stem: In the adjoining figure circle with centre D touches the sides of \(\angle ACB\) at A and B. If \(\angle ACB = 52^\circ\), find measure of \(\angle ADB\).
solution:
The sum of all angles of a quadrilateral is \(360^\circ\).

\(\therefore \angle ACB + \angle CAD + \angle CBD + \angle ADB = 360^\circ\)

\(\therefore 52^\circ + 90^\circ + 90^\circ + \angle ADB = 360^\circ\) ............ Tangent theorem

\(\therefore \angle ADB + 232^\circ = 360^\circ\)

\(\therefore \angle ADB = 360^\circ - 232^\circ = 128^\circ\)
note: Book's first worked example under the 'Solved Examples' banner on printed p.53; it is labelled 'Ex. (1)' while its sibling on p.54 is labelled 'Eg. (2)' — the book is inconsistent about the label, not about the numbering.

stem: Point O is the centre of a circle. Line \(a\) and line \(b\) are parallel tangents to the circle at P and Q. Prove that segment PQ is a diameter of the circle.
solution:
Draw a line \(c\) through O which is parallel to line \(a\). Draw radii OQ and OP.

Now, \(\angle OPT = 90^\circ\) ..... Tangent theorem

\(\therefore \angle SOP = 90^\circ\) ... Int. angle property ... (I)

line \(a \parallel\) line \(c\) ..... construction

line \(a \parallel\) line \(b\) ..... given

\(\therefore\) line \(b \parallel\) line \(c\)

\(\therefore \angle SOQ = 90^\circ\) ... Int. angle property ...(II)

\(\therefore\) From (I) and (II),

\(\angle SOP + \angle SOQ = 90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ\)

\(\therefore\) ray OP and ray OQ are opposite rays.

\(\therefore\) P, O, Q are collinear points.

\(\therefore\) seg PQ is a diameter of the circle.
note: In the book's figure 3.18 the auxiliary line \(c\) meets line \(a\) at T and line \(b\) at R, and S is the point where line \(c\) crosses to the right of O; the printed solution names T and S without introducing them in the statement.

subtopic: Measure of an Arc and Central Angle
stem:
A, B, C are any points on the circle with centre O.

(i) Write the names of all arcs formed due to these points.

(ii) If \(m\) arc (BC) \(= 110^\circ\) and \(m\) arc (AB) \(= 125^\circ\), find measures of all remaining arcs.
solution:
(i) Names of arcs -

arc AB, arc BC, arc AC, arc ABC, arc ACB, arc BAC

(ii) \(m(\text{arc ABC}) = m(\text{arc AB}) + m(\text{arc BC})\)

\(= 125^\circ + 110^\circ = 235^\circ\)

\(m(\text{arc AC}) = 360^\circ - m(\text{arc ACB})\)

\(= 360^\circ - 235^\circ = 125^\circ\)

Similarly, \(m(\text{arc ACB}) = 360^\circ - 125^\circ = 235^\circ\)

and \(m(\text{arc BAC}) = 360^\circ - 110^\circ = 250^\circ\)
note: In the printed solution the third line reads "m(arc AC) = 360 - m(arc ACB)"; the arc opposite to arc AC is arc ABC, so the citation should be m(arc ABC). Here m(arc ACB) happens to equal 235 as well, so the printed value 125 is correct and the slip does not change the answer. Transcribed as printed.

stem:
In the figure 3.36 a rectangle PQRS is inscribed in a circle with centre T. Prove that,

(i) arc PQ \(\cong\) arc SR

(ii) arc SPQ \(\cong\) arc PQR
solution:
(i) \(\square\)PQRS in a rectangle.

\(\therefore\) chord PQ \(\cong\) chord SR ....... opposite sides of a rectangle

\(\therefore\) arc PQ \(\cong\) arc SR ...... arcs corresponding to congruent chords.

(ii) chord PS \(\cong\) chord QR ..... Opposite sides of a rectangle

\(\therefore\) arc SP \(\cong\) arc QR ..... arcs corresponding to congruent chords.

\(\therefore\) measures of arcs SP and QR are equal

Now, \(m(\text{arc SP}) + m(\text{arc PQ}) = m(\text{arc PQ}) + m(\text{arc QR})\)

\(\therefore m(\text{arc SPQ}) = m(\text{arc PQR})\)

\(\therefore\) arc SPQ \(\cong\) arc PQR
note: The printed solution opens "PQRS in a rectangle" — 'in' is a misprint for 'is'. Transcribed as printed.

stem:
In figure 3.51, chord LM \(\cong\) chord LN, \(\angle L = 35^\circ\) find

(i) \(m(\text{arc MN})\)

(ii) \(m(\text{arc LN})\)
solution:
(i) \(\angle L = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc MN})\) ......inscribed angle theorem.

\(\therefore 35 = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc MN})\)

\(\therefore 2 \times 35 = m(\text{arc MN}) = 70^\circ\)

(ii) \(m(\text{arc MLN}) = 360^\circ - m(\text{arc MN})\) ...... definition of measure of arc

\(= 360^\circ - 70^\circ = 290^\circ\)

Now, chord LM \(\cong\) chord LN

\(\therefore\) arc LM \(\cong\) arc LN

but \(m(\text{arc LM}) + m(\text{arc LN}) = m(\text{arc MLN}) = 290^\circ\) ..... arc addition property

\(m(\text{arc LM}) = m(\text{arc LN}) = \dfrac{290^\circ}{2} = 145^\circ\)

or, (ii) chord LM \(\cong\) chord LN

\(\therefore \angle M = \angle N\) ...... isosceles trinangle theorem.

\(\therefore 2\angle M = 180^\circ - 35^\circ = 145^\circ\)

\(\therefore \angle M = \dfrac{145^\circ}{2}\)

Now, \(m(\text{arc LN}) = 2 \times \angle M\)

\(= 2 \times \dfrac{145^\circ}{2} = 145^\circ\)
note: The book prints "isosceles trinangle theorem" — a misprint for 'triangle'. Transcribed as printed. The solution runs from printed p.70 onto p.71.

ref: Converse of cyclic quadrilateral theorem SolvedEx.2
stem:
In figure 3.52, chords PQ and RS intersect at T.

(i) Find \(m(\text{arc SQ})\) if \(m\angle STQ = 58^\circ\), \(m\angle PSR = 24^\circ\).

(ii) Verify, \(\angle STQ = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc PR}) + m(\text{arc SQ})\right]\)

(iii) Prove that : \(\angle STQ = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc PR}) + m(\text{arc SQ})\right]\) for any measure of \(\angle STQ\).

(iv) Write in words the property in (iii).
solution:
(i) \(\angle SPQ = \angle SPT = 58^\circ - 24^\circ = 34^\circ\) ....... exterior angle theorem.

\(m(\text{arc QS}) = 2\angle SPQ = 2 \times 34^\circ = 68^\circ\)

(ii) \(m(\text{arc PR}) = 2\angle PSR = 2 \times 24^\circ = 48^\circ\)

Now, \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc PR}) + m(\text{arc SQ})\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[48 + 68\right]\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 116 = 58^\circ\)

\(= \angle STQ\)

(iii) The book prints this step as a fill-in-the-blanks proof; the blanks are completed here.

\(\angle STQ = \angle SPQ + \angle PSR\) ....... exterior angle theorem of a triangle

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc SQ}) + \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc PR})\) ....... inscribed angle theorem

\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc SQ}) + m(\text{arc PR})\right]\)

(iv) If two chords of a circle intersect each other in the interior of a circle then the measure of the angle between them is half the sum of measures of arcs intercepted by the angle and its opposite angle.
note: Part (iii) is printed with four empty boxes for the student to fill; the completed steps are supplied so the stored model answer is a whole proof rather than a hole. Parts (i), (ii) and (iv) are transcribed exactly as printed.

ref: Converse of cyclic quadrilateral theorem SolvedEx.3
stem: Prove that, if two lines containing chords of a circle intersect each other outside the circle, then the measure of angle between them is half the difference in measures of the arcs intercepted by the angle.
solution:
Given : Chords AB and CD intersect at E in the exterior of the circle.

To prove : \(\angle AEC = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc AC}) - m(\text{arc BD})\right]\)

Construction : Draw seg AD.

Proof : The book leaves this proof to the student, directing: "Consider angles of \(\triangle AED\) and its exterior angle and write the proof." It is completed here.

\(\angle ADC\) is an exterior angle of \(\triangle AED\) at D.

\(\therefore \angle ADC = \angle AED + \angle DAE\) ....... exterior angle theorem of a triangle

\(\therefore \angle AEC = \angle ADC - \angle DAB\) ....... (\(\angle AED\) is \(\angle AEC\) and \(\angle DAE\) is \(\angle DAB\))

Now \(\angle ADC\) is inscribed in the circle and intercepts arc AC,

\(\therefore \angle ADC = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc AC})\) ....... inscribed angle theorem

and \(\angle DAB\) intercepts arc BD,

\(\therefore \angle DAB = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc BD})\) ....... inscribed angle theorem

\(\therefore \angle AEC = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc AC}) - \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc BD})\)

\(\therefore \angle AEC = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc AC}) - m(\text{arc BD})\right]\)
note: The book prints only the statement, Given, To prove and Construction, and asks the student to write the proof. The proof is supplied here so the stored model answer is complete; the Given / To prove / Construction lines are the book's own.

solution:
\(PS^2 = PQ \times PR\) .... tangent secant segments theorem

\(= 3.6 \times [3.6 + 6.4]\)

\(= 3.6 \times 10\)

\(\therefore PS = 6\)

stem: In figure 3.74, chord MN and chord RS intersect each other at point P. If PR = 6, PS = 4, MN = 11 find PN.
solution:
By theorem on interesecting chords,

\(PN \times PM = PR \times PS\)... (I)

let \(PN = x\). \(\therefore PM = 11 - x\)

substituting the values in (I),

\(x(11 - x) = 6 \times 4\)

\(\therefore 11x - x^2 - 24 = 0\)

\(\therefore x^2 - 11x + 24 = 0\)

\(\therefore (x - 3)(x - 8) = 0\)

\(\therefore x - 3 = 0\) or \(x - 8 = 0\)

\(\therefore x = 3\) or \(x = 8\)

\(\therefore PN = 3\) or \(PN = 8\)
note: The book prints "interesecting" — a misprint for 'intersecting'. Transcribed as printed.

stem: In figure 3.75, two circles intersect each other in points X and Y. Tangents drawn from a point M on line XY touch the circles at P and Q. Prove that, seg PM \(\cong\) seg QM.
solution:
The book prints this proof with blanks for the student to fill; the blanks are completed here.

Line MX is a common secant of the two circles.

\(\therefore PM^2 = MY \times MX\) ..... (I)

Similarly \(QM^2 = MY \times MX\), tangent secant segment theorem ......(II)

\(\therefore\) From (I) and (II) \(PM^2 = QM^2\)

\(\therefore PM = QM\)

seg PM \(\cong\) seg QM
note: Printed as a fill-in-the-blanks proof ("Line MX is a common ........ of the two circles", "Similarly ....... = ....... x ....... ", "From (I) and (II) ...... = QM^2"). The blanks are filled so the stored model answer is a whole proof; every other line is the book's own.

stem: In figure 3.76, seg PQ is a diameter of a circle with centre O. R is any point on the circle. seg RS \(\perp\) seg PQ. Prove that, SR is the geometric mean of PS and SQ. [That is, \(SR^2 = PS \times SQ\)]
solution:
The book gives only the four steps of the plan; the proof is written out here following them.

(1) Draw ray RS. It intersects the circle at T.

(2) Show that RS = TS.

seg PQ is a diameter and seg RT \(\perp\) seg PQ at S,

\(\therefore\) seg PQ bisects chord RT ....... the perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to its chord bisects the chord

\(\therefore RS = TS\) ..... (I)

(3) Chords RT and PQ intersect each other at S in the interior of the circle,

\(\therefore RS \times ST = PS \times SQ\) ....... theorem of internal division of chords ..... (II)

(4) From (I) and (II),

\(RS \times RS = PS \times SQ\)

\(\therefore SR^2 = PS \times SQ\)

\(\therefore\) SR is the geometric mean of PS and SQ.
note: The book prints "Solution : Write the proof with the help of the following steps" and lists four steps rather than a worked proof. The four steps are the book's own; the derivation under them is supplied so the stored model answer is complete.
